items.title: 10.1 Force on a current-carrying conductor in a uniform magnetic field

source_refs.note: Topic 10.1 with Figs. 10.2 to 10.4, Example 10.1 and the side boxes (PDF 230-232, printed 227-229). The print's description of Fig. 10.2 (force to the left with N above S and current out of the page) is flagged for review.

blocks.text: It has been observed experimentally that a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force. Consider a straight conductor carrying a steady current, placed perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field, with the current directed out of the paper (Fig. 10.2). Just as two magnets exert forces on each other through their magnetic fields, a current-carrying conductor experiences a force due to the interaction between its own magnetic field and the external magnetic field.

blocks.alt: A conductor seen end-on, with a dot showing the current out of the paper, sits between two pole blocks: S above and N below. Vertical field lines run upward from N to S. Blue circles with anticlockwise arrows show the conductor's own field. A force arrow F points horizontally to the left.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.2: A current-carrying conductor in a uniform magnetic field: current out of the paper and force F (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.2).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 10.2 puts N above S, which makes the field point downward; with the current out of the paper the force F = I L x B would then point to the right. To match the text's force to the left, the poles are drawn with S above and N below (field upward).

The magnetic field produced by the current and the external uniform field reinforce each other on one side of the conductor and cancel each other on the other side. Consequently the conductor moves towards the side where the field is weaker, that is, to the left (Fig. 10.2). Thus the force F is perpendicular to both the conductor and the magnetic field.

blocks.title: Fleming's left-hand rule
blocks.text: Position your left hand such that the first finger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the second finger points in the direction of the current; the thumb will then point in the direction of the force (Fig. 10.3). The direction of the force can also be found with the right-hand rule: curl the fingers of the right hand from the current to the magnetic field through the small angle; the stretched thumb indicates the direction of the force.

blocks.alt: A left hand with the thumb pointing straight up, labelled Force; the first finger pointing to the upper right, labelled Magnetic Field; and the second finger pointing to the lower right, labelled Current. The three are at right angles to one another; the other two fingers are folded.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.3: Fleming's left-hand rule (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.3).

blocks.alt: A bar magnet, S half green on the left and N half red on the right, with curved field lines leaving the N end and returning to the S end; arrows on the lines point away from N and towards S, and the lines do not cross.
blocks.caption: Do You Know? (PDF page 230): Magnetic field lines of a bar magnet (original drawing after the textbook's picture in this box).

blocks.text: Experimentally, the magnitude of the force on a conductor placed inside a magnetic field is directly proportional to the current I in the conductor, the length L of the conductor and the strength of the external magnetic field B. The strength of the magnetic field is also known as the magnetic induction B, which has the same direction as the field. Thus the force on a conductor of length L carrying a current I placed perpendicular to a field of strength B is F proportional to BIL, or F = kBIL. In SI units k = 1, therefore F = BIL ... (10.1).

blocks.title: Magnetic induction (field strength) B
blocks.text: From Eq. 10.1, B = F/IL: the magnetic field strength is numerically equal to the force exerted on a conductor of length one metre carrying a current of one ampere placed perpendicular to the magnetic field. The SI unit of B is the tesla (T): 1 T = 1 N A^-1 m^-1. Magnetic induction is a vector quantity whose direction is that of the magnetic field.

We can also consider a vector L whose magnitude equals the length of the conductor and whose direction is along the flow of current. If the conductor makes an angle theta with the magnetic field, we use the component of L perpendicular to B, that is L sin theta (Fig. 10.4). Then Eq. 10.1 becomes F = BIL sin theta ... (10.2). In vector form, F = I L x B ... (10.3). Equation 10.2 shows that the force is maximum (BIL) when the conductor is perpendicular to the field (theta = 90 degrees) and zero when the conductor lies along the field (theta = 0).

blocks.alt: From one point, vector B points straight up and vector L points up to the right at angle theta from B. A horizontal arrow from the same point, labelled L sin theta, ends directly below the tip of L, joined to it by a dashed vertical line.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.4: The component L sin theta of L perpendicular to B (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.4).

blocks.text: The Earth's magnetic field is approximately that of a dipole, like that of a fictitious bar magnet whose south magnetic pole is towards the geographic north pole and whose north magnetic pole is towards the geographic south pole (Interesting Information).

blocks.alt: The Earth with a fictitious bar magnet inside, tilted slightly from the geographic axis (dashed). Field lines loop round the Earth from its southern half to its northern half like those of a dipole. Labels: South magnetic pole and Geographic North pole at the top; Geographic South pole and North magnetic pole at the bottom.
blocks.caption: Interesting Information (PDF page 231): The Earth's magnetic field is approximately that of a dipole (original drawing after the textbook's picture in this box).

blocks.title: Example 10.1
blocks.text: A 20.0 cm wire carrying a current of 10.0 A is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.30 T. If the wire makes an angle of 40 degrees with the direction of the magnetic field, find the magnitude of the force acting on the wire. Solution: L = 20.0 cm = 0.20 m, I = 10.0 A, B = 0.30 T, theta = 40 degrees. Substituting in Eq. 10.2: F = 10.0 A x 0.30 T x 0.20 m x sin 40 degrees = 0.39 N.
